title: File Handling
description: Reading and writing files safely with open(), file modes, and the with statement.
objectives: Open files in the correct mode for the task
Read and write text and binary files
Use the with statement for automatic cleanup

content.heading: Opening and Reading Files
content.body:
open(path, mode) returns a file object. Common modes: "r" (read text, default, error if the file doesn't exist), "w" (write text, creates the file or truncates an existing one), "a" (append text to the end), and their binary counterparts "rb"/"wb"/"ab" for non-text data. read() returns the entire file's contents as one string; readline() reads one line at a time; readlines() returns a list of all lines. Iterating directly over a file object (for line in f:) is the most memory-efficient way to process a large file line by line, since it doesn't load the whole file into memory at once.

For writing, write(text) writes a single string (it does not add a newline automatically — you must include \n yourself), and writelines(list_of_strings) writes each string in the list in sequence (also without inserting newlines between them).

content.heading: with, Encoding, and Common Errors
content.body:
The with statement is the standard, idiomatic way to work with files: with open(path) as f: ... automatically calls f.close() when the block exits, even if an exception occurs inside it — this guarantees the file handle is released and any buffered writes are flushed. Forgetting to close a file (or not using with) can leave writes unflushed or exhaust the OS's limit on open file handles in a long-running program.

For text files, specifying encoding="utf-8" explicitly (open(path, "r", encoding="utf-8")) avoids relying on the platform's default encoding, which can differ between systems. Common file errors include FileNotFoundError (opening a missing file for reading), PermissionError (insufficient OS permissions), and IsADirectoryError (opening a directory as if it were a file) — these are all subclasses of OSError and can be caught accordingly.

content.explanation: The with statement guarantees the file is closed after each block, even though there's no explicit f.close() call. strip() removes the trailing newline each readline includes.

keyPoints: "r"/"w"/"a" are the core text modes; add "b" for binary data
with open(...) as f: guarantees the file is closed, even on an exception
write() does not add newlines automatically — include \n explicitly
Specify encoding="utf-8" explicitly for portable text file handling
commonMistakes: Opening a file without with and forgetting to close it
Opening a file in "r" mode and then trying to write to it
Not catching FileNotFoundError when a file's existence isn't guaranteed
